newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN reparations body for Gulf War lacks funds. [CORRECTED 14:36 GMT]
newsitem.headline: UN reparations body for Gulf War lacks funds. [CORRECTED 14:36 GMT]

text.p: The U.N. reparations fund for the Gulf War will have approved roughly $7 billion in awards to claimants by the end of 1996, but lacks funds to make payments to victims before then, its executive secretary said on Tuesday.
Carlos Alzamora, executive secretary of the United Nations Compensation Commission, blamed the latest funding crisis on the delay in implementing the oil-for-food accord with Iraq.
But he expected the elusive deal to go ahead in December.
"I presume maybe sometime in December. That has been the forecast," he told reporters, making clear it was a U.N. timetable.
Alzamora said he was trying to avoid the cash-strapped Commission running out of cash next April, possibly through a bridging loan from major Western donor countries.
Alzamora, a 70-year-old former Peruvian diplomat, also told reporters that he was retiring by year-end.
Asked whether the fund would be able to pay out awards to claimants this year, he replied: "By now it is too late to think we could make substantial payments by the end of the year.
"We are ready to start the payments as soon as the money is there. By the end of the year we would have issued awards for close to $7 billion," he added.
"When you look back at history, this has been the rule, never the exception. We have to adapt to realities."

The Commission, set up by the Security Council to compensate direct losses caused by Iraq's invasion and occupation of Kuwait in 1990-91, is processing claims from individuals, companies and governments against Baghdad worth an asserted $200 billion.

But the "oil-for-food deal" under resolution 986, which would allow Baghdad to sell $2 billion of oil over six months to buy food and medicine, has been delayed -- spoiling the Commission's hopes to pay out awards to individual claimants.
The Geneva-based body, which is due to receive 30 per cent of the revenue generated by the limited Iraqi oil sales, expected to get $100 million a month from the deal.
Alzamora said only $10 million was left in the Commission's coffers, enough to cover expenses through April, but he said he was seeking alternative sources of funding to bridge the gap.
"We expect to find a solution in time so we can proceed with this operation...We trust that in these coming weeks a solution will be found," he said.
"Maybe a group of donors who would provide bridging funds until one of these permanent solutions is found. Efforts are being coordinated by several countries," he said, declining to give details.
Alzamora said he had made a "special appeal" to the 15 member states of the Commission's Governing Council, composed of the same members of the U.N. Security Council.

He spoke as the Commission's 15-member Governing Council, were winding up a two-day meeting to approve $320 million in awards to 80,450 individuals forced to flee Kuwait or Iraq due to the invasion. A total of 920,873 people in this "forced departure" category will have been awarded $3.2 billion.

To date, the Commission has only been able to pay out $13.4 million (Corrects from billion) in awards to 4,000 priority claimants for death of a close relative or serious injury. Funds came from government donations and seized Iraqi assets.
"I am going to leave the Commission at the end of the year. I think I have made my contribution," Alzamora said.
"I think things are on track," he added. "I hope to leave it perhaps in a better financial situation."
